newsitem.title: USA: TWA crash 6 months old, but no cause yet found.
newsitem.headline: TWA crash 6 months old, but no cause yet found.

text.p: TWA Flight 800 exploded and crashed six months ago, but investigators remain in a quandary over its cause -- mechanical failure of the Boeing 747, a bomb or a missile.

The investigators said Thursday that their probe of the July 17 crash off New York's Long Island which killed all 230 people on board was continuing, and they pledged to take every step necessary to find out why it happened.
James Hall, chairman of the National Transportation Safety Board, said "We have identified a possible mechanism that could lead to a center wing tank explosion."
But, he told the White House Commission on Aviation Safety and Security, "We do not know if this occurred on Flight 800."
He said "Three theories, bomb, missile and mechanical failure, remain," adding, however, that "to date there is no evidence of a bomb or missile."
Board investigators, sources say, are gradually turning away from a terrorist act and toward mechanical failure.

The Paris-bound 747 exploded shortly after takeoff from Kennedy airport. Investigators have dredged up almost all of the wreckage, and reassembled much of it in a vacant hangar on Long Island to sift for clues to the explosion and crash.
Trawlers continue to search the ocean bottom.

Board investigators have said they have located the explosion in the center fuel tank, apparently from ignition of fuel fumes. The source of ignition has not been determined, but static electricity is one theory being considered.
Hall said several mechanical scenarios were being investigated, but he gave no details.

The NTSB chief is a member of the White House commission and was asked by commissiom chairman, Vice President Al Gore, to give a recap of the Flight 800 investigation before the opening of one of the panel's regular meetings.
The panel was formed after the crash to try to find ways to improve aviation and airport safety and security.
Further tests are planned, Hall said, including several centered on the bomb and missile theories. They would include building a three-dimentional mock-up of the structure around a center fuel tank.
There would also be jet fuel tests to study the fuel's explosive force, and once that was done, "large scale tests involving the Boeing 747 and its fuel tanks are likely."
